opus-5.5.text:
So the basic logic is this. If your argument that a model is safe to deploy rests on the claim "this model doesn't have harmful tendencies," that claim is doing a lot of work. You'd better have some evidence for it, and ideally evidence you gather before the model is out in the world, because after deployment it's much harder to walk things back.

It helps to separate two kinds of safety arguments. One is an inability argument: the model just can't do the dangerous thing, it lacks the capability. The other is a propensity or alignment argument: maybe the model could do something harmful, but it won't, because its tendencies don't point that way. Inability arguments are relatively easy to test. You run capability evals, and if the model can't do the task even when you try hard to elicit it, that's fairly strong evidence. Propensity arguments are much trickier. You're making a claim about what the model is disposed to do across a huge range of situations, including ones you haven't seen.

Pre-deployment evals are one of the main ways to get traction on that. You put the model in situations designed to tempt or pressure it toward bad behavior, such as opportunities to deceive, to pursue some goal at the expense of what the developer wants, or to undermine oversight. Then you see what it does. If it consistently behaves well, that's some evidence. If it doesn't, you've learned something important before anyone is relying on it.

I want to be honest about the limitations, though. A clean result on propensity evals is weaker evidence than a clean result on capability evals. Your scenarios might not resemble the real situations where things would go wrong. And as models get more capable, there's a real concern that a model could recognize it's being evaluated and behave differently. That's part of why I don't think evals alone should carry a safety case once models are capable enough. You want them combined with other lines of evidence, like interpretability, careful monitoring after deployment, and control measures that would catch problems even if the alignment assessment turns out to be wrong.

Still, I'd say they're necessary even if they aren't sufficient. If you're claiming a model lacks harmful tendencies and you haven't seriously tried to elicit those tendencies before deploying it, you don't really have a safety case. You have a hope.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating harmful tendencies and limits of propensity tests, but does not state that small changes in post-training can substantially change a model’s propensity for harmful behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin Shah: So the way I think about it is that a safety case is basically an argument for why you shouldn't expect a particular deployment to lead to catastrophic outcomes. And there are a few different shapes that argument can take. One shape is "the model isn't capable enough to cause the harm, even if it tried." Another is "the model is capable enough, but we have control measures that would catch it if it tried." And then a third is "the model is capable enough, and maybe we don't fully trust our control measures, but we have good reason to believe the model doesn't have the tendency to try in the first place."

That third one is the one where pre-deployment evaluations really do a lot of work, because the whole argument rests on an empirical claim about what the model is disposed to do. You can't just assert it. You have to go and check. And the only time you can check in a relatively clean way is before the model is out in the world, when you control the conditions, you can put it in a bunch of situations that would be tempting if it did have harmful tendencies, and see what it actually does.

Once you deploy, a couple of things change. One is that the stakes are now real: if the model does have a tendency to, say, pursue some goal that's misaligned with what the developers intended, the cost of discovering that after deployment is much higher than discovering it in a sandbox. The second is that it becomes much harder to interpret what you're seeing. In deployment you have this enormous distribution of inputs, you don't control them, and you often don't know what the model would have done in the counterfactual. So if you want to say "we looked and we didn't see the harmful tendency," pre-deployment is where that evidence is cleanest.

I'd also say there's a subtlety here, which is that evaluations of tendencies are harder than evaluations of capabilities. For capabilities, you're trying to elicit the best the model can do, and if you fail to elicit it, you at least know which direction you're wrong in. For tendencies, you're asking "what does the model do by default, in a situation that looks like real deployment?" And the model might behave differently if it can tell it's being evaluated. So part of why these evals matter is not just that you run them, but that running them well forces you to confront questions like: does the model know it's in a test? Are our scenarios realistic enough? Are we actually sampling from the situations that matter? If your safety case depends on the model's lack of harmful tendencies, those questions are load-bearing, and you'd much rather have grappled with them before deployment than be surprised afterwards.

So the short version is: if your argument for safety is "the model is fine," then at some point you have to produce evidence that the model is fine, and pre-deployment evaluation is the main place you get to produce that evidence under conditions you understand.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating harmful tendencies before deployment, but does not state that small post-training changes can substantially alter a model’s propensity for harmful behavior.

astra-6.text:
Well, if your safety case is that the model doesn’t have harmful tendencies, you need evidence about how the model actually behaves. You can’t just point to the fact that you trained it to be helpful and harmless and conclude that the training succeeded.

Pre-deployment evaluations let you put pressure on that claim. You can deliberately construct situations where a harmful tendency would be more likely to show up, and see what happens. If the model behaves badly, that’s a reason to revise your safety case before exposing people to the risk.

The tricky part is interpreting a clean result. Not finding a harmful tendency isn’t the same as showing that it isn’t there. Maybe your tests didn’t create the right circumstances, or maybe the model behaves differently in evaluation than it would in deployment. So you also need an argument that, if the tendency existed, your evaluations would have had a good chance of detecting it. That’s what makes the results meaningful evidence for the safety case.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations can reveal harmful tendencies and that training alone does not prove they are absent, but it does not state that small post-training changes can substantially alter a model’s propensity for harmful behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if your safety case rests on the claim that the model doesn’t have harmful tendencies, you need some evidence for that claim before you deploy it. You can’t just say, “We trained it to be helpful, and we haven’t noticed anything worrying.” You want to put it in situations where those tendencies would have a chance to show up and see what it does.

The tricky thing is that not observing a harmful behavior isn’t the same as establishing that the model won’t do it. Maybe your tests didn’t create the right circumstances. Maybe the model couldn’t carry out the harmful action in your test environment, even though it could with the tools it will have after deployment. So the evaluation needs to connect to the actual argument you’re making: what behavior are you ruling out, under what conditions, and how much evidence does passing the test really provide?

I’d think of pre-deployment evaluations as a way to scrutinize that premise of the safety case. They can uncover reasons it’s wrong, and well-designed tests can give you more confidence in it. But passing an evaluation shouldn’t turn a conditional, uncertain claim into a blanket assurance of safety.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing for harmful tendencies and limits of evaluation, but does not state that small post-training changes can substantially alter a model’s propensity for harmful behavior.
